consistency_checks.detail: Obesity, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, and pre‑diabetes all present and meet ATP‑III criteria.
Creatinine is elevated but eGFR and albuminuria are missing; CKD diagnosis is plausible but not fully substantiated.
Leukopenia is linked only to viral infection and MDS; more common causes such as chronic inflammation or medication effect are not addressed.
Attributed solely to adrenal insufficiency; alternative explanations (early CKD, nutritional factors, medication timing) are omitted.

critical_findings_addressed: Leukopenia (WBC 3.8 ×10³/µL) – addressed by viral infection, MDS, and hematologic differentials
Fasting hypoglycaemia (glucose 67.6 mg/dL) – addressed by primary adrenal insufficiency
Borderline hyperkalaemia (K⁺ 5.1 mmol/L) – addressed by CKD and adrenal insufficiency
top_concerns: Probability weighting for several low‑likelihood diagnoses (viral infection, adrenal insufficiency, MDS) is too high.
Missing essential laboratory work‑up (eGFR, urine ACR, iron studies, cortisol/ACTH, B12, folate, thyroid panel).
CKD is presented as a primary diagnosis rather than a complication of metabolic syndrome.
Leukopenia and hypoglycaemia are not fully explained by common causes.
Absence of screening for obstructive sleep apnea symptoms and nutritional deficiencies.
review_summary: The differential captures the core metabolic picture and includes relevant complications, but probability calibration is off, key work‑up results are missing, and critical findings (leukopenia, hypoglycaemia) lack parsimonious explanations. Re‑ranking with metabolic syndrome as primary and early CKD as the main complication, plus targeted low‑cost labs, will improve diagnostic accuracy.
